# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was an influential computer scientist and electrical engineer notable for her pioneering work in supercomputer architecture and very-large-scale integration (VLSI) chip design. After earning her B.S. and M.S.E.E. from Columbia University in the early 1960s, she joined IBM Research, where she contributed to the Advanced Computing Systems project and pioneered techniques such as multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling, laying groundwork for superscalar architectures.
Conway’s gender transition led to her dismissal from IBM in 1968; decades later, the company publicly apologized and honored her contributions. Post-transition, she resumed her career at Computer Applications, Inc., Memorex, and Xerox PARC, where she founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and co-developed the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology. Their textbook became a standard for chip design, and Conway’s innovations facilitated rapid prototyping infrastructures like MOSIS. She also taught at MIT and later joined DARPA and the University of Michigan. Recognized for her technical achievements as well as her advocacy for transgender rights, Conway received numerous awards including IEEE Fellow, National Academy of Engineering membership, and the IEEE Computer Society’s Computer Pioneer Award. She coined the “Conway effect” to describe historical overlooking of marginalized innovators. Conway died in 2024 at age 86.
